newsitem.title: GERMANY: Coconut oil price in Europe seen firm, then easing.
newsitem.headline: Coconut oil price in Europe seen firm, then easing.

text.p: Lauric oil sector sources in Europe said shipment delays at origin were underpinning nearby prices but the forward months should ease along with increasingly comfortable supply fundamentals.
"We've heard a ship from the Philippines was delayed and could not leave in May and had to be replaced," a northern European importer said.
"The replacement will only be able to load during the first eight days of June and that is causing high spot prices in Europe...but the problems could be over in two weeks."
Traders said coconut prices had fallen by around $80 per tonne in May under the impression of looming supply additions in the second half of 1997.
The latest reaction to shipment problems showed trade and consumer supplies were tight after all and demand was high.
One major swing consumer is the oleochemical industry, as food demand for coconut oil is fairly static.
The industry has been replacing coconut oil with palmkernel oil, other vegetable oils or synthetic oils, and this has contributed to the most recent price decline in coconut oil.
PKO showed a small premium over coconut oil in Europe today, with Malaysian/Indonesian May/June material at $675 a tonnes and Philippine/Indonesian May/June coconut oil at $670.
Philippine coconut export officials on Monday said major consumers Henkel KGaA and U.S.-based Procter & Gamble Co had switched to alternatives earlier this year when export supplies were still short.
Exporters in Manila said they wanted to win them back.
But traders said Malaysian crude palmkernel oil prices in ringgit were highly competitive to industrial users here and coconut oil sellers would need to take this on board.
Staff at Henkel in Duesseldorf said buyers authorised to comment on strategy were unavailable for comment this week.

The Oil World newsletter, meanwhile, forecast Philippine coconut oil exports in the 1997 calendar year at 830,000 tonnes, up 200,000 from 1996, citing a sharp increase in export availability from June onwards.
"We expect a sizeable increase in these exports, regardless of the latest shipping delay," said editor Thomas Mielke.
"Major consumers will probably be able to bridge the gap."
